chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The deceased is enshrouded in three (pieces of cloth), besides the turban and the cloth with which he ties his hips so that nothing of him is exposed; and the cloth and the turban are essential, but they are not part of the shroud.

key_terms.الْخِرْقَةُ: The cloth or rag used to tie around the hips/waist
key_terms.الْعِمَامَةُ: The turban, worn on the head
key_terms.ثَلَاثَةٍ: Three (referring to the three main pieces of the shroud)
key_terms.كَفَنَ: To enshroud or wrap the deceased in cloth for burial

ai.seo_question: What are the required components and count for a Muslim's burial shroud according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the technical composition of the Islamic burial shroud by distinguishing between the three primary garments constituting the kafan and the auxiliary items like the turban and hip-cloth used for modesty and securing the body. In Shia jurisprudence, this distinction is crucial for determining the minimum legal requirements versus recommended practices, emphasizing that while the turban and hip-cloth are essential for proper preparation, they do not count toward the obligatory three pieces of cloth. This ruling reflects the scholarly emphasis on both the physical dignity of the deceased and the precise adherence to prophetic traditions in funeral rites.
